planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; give Redlands #4 extra elbow room compared with smaller jujube cultivars since its fruit size depends partly on vigorous, well-lit growth.

directions: Redlands #4 traces back to a chance seedling found on an old homestead in Redlands, California, and is grown chiefly for producing some of the largest round fruit of any jujube cultivar, exceeding the size of the widely planted Li. The flesh is crisp and richly flavored when harvested at the green-to-yellow stage for fresh eating, with texture and sugar content that hold up well through the mahogany-brown stage if left to fully ripen and semi-dry on the tree. Because jujube trees sucker readily from root fragments, plant Redlands #4 where root disturbance from nearby digging or tilling can be avoided, and pair it with a second cultivar such as Li or Lang to encourage heavier fruit set through cross-pollination. Once established, the tree tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with little intervention, making it a low-maintenance choice for a large specimen jujube.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Jujube Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension
University of California Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; because Winter Delight ripens late in the season, site it where it gets uninterrupted sun into autumn to help the crop finish before hard frost.

directions: Winter Delight is one of several jujube selections imported from northern China by Oregon nurseryman Jim Gilbert, valued for its compact, naturally tidy tree and crisp, egg-shaped fruit that ripens toward the tail end of the jujube season. Because a major nursery mislabeled Autumn Beauty as Winter Delight years ago, some plants sold under the name actually ripen earlier than expected, so confirm fruiting time with the source nursery if season length matters for your planting plan. The tree is markedly cold-hardy and tolerates the poor, dry soils typical of the species, needing little more than an occasional deep watering during establishment. Fruit is best harvested at the crisp green-to-tan stage for fresh eating, or left to fully brown and wrinkle for a chewier, date-like texture.
sources: Oregon State University Extension Service
One Green World nursery variety notes
California Rare Fruit Growers — Jujube Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; So stays small enough that it can be grown in a large container or a tight urban lot without crowding neighboring plantings.

directions: So is a relatively recent Chinese cultivar prized for fruit that many jujube growers rank among the sweetest of any variety, though it carries a distinctive tart undertone that sets it apart from straightforwardly sugary types like Honey Jar. The round fruit stays small, under an inch across, and the tree itself grows compact and naturally tidy, making it a good option where space is limited. Unlike many jujube cultivars that benefit from a cross-pollinator, So sets a reliable crop on its own, simplifying planting decisions for a single-tree yard. Harvest at the crisp yellow-green to tan stage for the best balance of sweetness and tang, since the tart note fades and the fruit turns simply sweet as it fully browns.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Jujube Fruit Facts
New Mexico State University Extension — Jujube: Chinese Date in New Mexico
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Massandra's early ripening window suits gardeners in shorter-season climates who want a reliable harvest before fall's first cold snap.

directions: Massandra originated at the Nikita Botanical Garden near Yalta on Ukraine's Crimean coast, part of a Black Sea breeding tradition that also produced several other jujube selections grown for cold tolerance. The fruit is notably large for an early-ripening cultivar, with glossy, dark-brown skin at full maturity and a sweet, flavorful flesh that many growers compare favorably to standard Chinese selections. Trees bear heavily once established and tolerate the same poor, well-drained soils and drought that make jujube generally easy to grow, needing supplemental water mainly in the first year or two. Because Massandra shares ancestry with other Black Sea-region cultivars, plant it alongside a genetically distinct variety such as Li or Lang if maximizing fruit set is a priority.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Jujube Fruit Facts
One Green World nursery variety notes
USDA National Plant Germplasm System

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; the naturally compact, contorted branching makes ZigZag a good candidate for a small-space ornamental-edible planting near a patio or entry.

directions: ZigZag is grown as much for its winter silhouette as for its fruit, with branches that kink sharply at each node to create a strikingly angular, sculptural form once the leaves drop in fall. Fruit is large for the species and turns a deep chocolate-brown at full ripeness, with a sweet, apple-like flavor typical of well-ripened jujube. The tree stays naturally compact and is partially self-fertile, though planting a second cultivar such as Autumn Beauty nearby improves both fruit set and size. Like other jujube selections, ZigZag develops a deep taproot early on and becomes strongly drought-tolerant once past its first year or two in the ground.
sources: One Green World nursery variety notes
California Rare Fruit Growers — Jujube Fruit Facts
Oregon State University Extension Service

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Coco's smaller mature size and attractive winter branching suit a mixed edible border as readily as a dedicated orchard row.

directions: Coco is notable among jujube cultivars for a fruit flavor many growers describe as distinctly coconut-like once the small, golden-brown fruit fully ripens, setting it apart from the more straightforwardly apple- or date-flavored cultivars in wider circulation. The zigzagging branch pattern gives the tree ornamental interest through the leafless winter months, and like most jujube it develops a deep taproot that makes it notably drought-tolerant once established. Trees typically begin bearing in their second or third year and are partially self-fertile, though fruit set and size improve with a second cultivar such as Autumn Beauty planted nearby for cross-pollination. Harvest when the skin turns golden-brown for the best expression of the variety's distinctive flavor, or let fruit fully wrinkle for a chewier, date-like texture.
sources: Phoenix Perennials nursery variety notes
California Rare Fruit Growers — Jujube Fruit Facts
USDA National Plant Germplasm System

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before moving them into full sun; Kentucky Champion is reported as self-fertile but still crops more heavily with a second, genetically distinct cultivar such as Sunflower or Susquehanna planted nearby.

directions: Kentucky Champion was discovered on a vigorous seedling tree near Richmond, Kentucky, and stands out among pawpaw cultivars for consistently ripening among the earliest of the commercially available named selections, often coloring up in September well ahead of many other cultivars. Fruit runs large, close to half a pound, with melon-orange flesh carrying a tropical flavor with a faint raspberry note, and a comparatively small proportion of seed to pulp that leaves more usable fruit per pick. The skin is thicker and more resistant to bruising and dark spotting than many older pawpaw selections, which helps it hold up better to handling and short-term storage. As with other pawpaw cultivars, young trees need light shade to establish before tolerating full sun, and pawpaw's odd, fly- and beetle-pollinated maroon flowers may need hand pollination with a small brush in gardens lacking those insects.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program
Journal of the American Pomological Society — Physical Characterization of North American Pawpaw Cultivars
Virginia Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained to average soil; Miller's spreading, drooping branch habit needs more lateral room than upright American persimmon selections, so allow generous spacing from structures and other trees.

directions: Miller is grown for producing some of the largest fruit known among American persimmon selections, regularly exceeding two and a half inches across, with color ranging from light yellow-orange to a deeper orange-red depending on the season and ripeness. The tree tends toward a multi-stemmed, wide-spreading form with drooping branches and foliage that give it a looser, almost tropical look compared with the more upright habit of many other native persimmon cultivars. It is vigorous and comes into bearing relatively early for the species, typically by its third year, and produces heavy annual crops once mature. Like all American persimmon, fruit must fully soften on the tree or be sweetened by a hard frost before eating, since unripe fruit is strongly astringent; drop typically runs from October into late November depending on region.
sources: The Dawes Arboretum — Diospyros virginiana 'Miller' variety records
Kentucky State University — American Persimmon Cultivar Trials
